records.author_body: I'm building GazeRank, a website audit tool for SEO, performance, accessibility, and AI search readiness. I'm a solo founder. The app has been online since August, but I only started sharing it publicly on October 1. The numbers so far • 12 signups in the database (4 are my own test accounts) • 3 users ran a scan • 0 came back on a different day • ~30 tracked visits since October 1, probably an undercount Five of the eight non-test signups never ran a scan. Traffic is still tiny, so I can't blame everything on activation. But activation is something I can work on this week. What I've tried • X: A pinned post and a thread sharing data from 285 website scans. A handful of comments. • LinkedIn: 292 impressions, 7 clicks, 0 reactions, and 2 comments on the company page. • Directories: Submitted to 8, including SaaSHub, AlternativeTo, and BetaList. • Product Hunt: Preparing for launch. The directories haven't had enough time to tell me much yet. One interesting finding I scanned 285 websites, mostly SaaS, developer-tool, and marketing sites. • 54% had no content freshness signal. • 52% had low readability. • 51% were missing at least one security header. These findings suggest the issues are common. They don't tell me whether people care enough to scan their own sites, let alone pay to fix them. Full methodology and data: https://www.gazerank.com/reports/benchmark One lesson from building the product Scanning my own site once showed a Performance score of 100 next to a poor Largest Contentful Paint (LCP). I fixed it and wrote about the experience. It reminded me that an audit tool needs to earn trust through evidence, not just scores. What I'm trying this week Email the five people who signed up but never scanned and ask what stopped them. Post from my personal LinkedIn profile instead of only the company page. Reply to every relevant comment with something useful, offering a scan where it makes sense. I'll share what I learn, including if none of it works. Two questions for founders who've been here What got your early signups to actually use your product? Was it a change to onboarding, a personal email, a demo, or something else? What was the first channel that brought you a user who returned the following week? What did you actually do that week? Concrete examples would help more than general advice. And if you'd like a GazeRank scan, drop your URL. I'll run it and share up to three useful findings where possible.

metadata.headline: 8 signups, 3 people scanned, 0 came back. How did you get your first users to stick?

records.author_body: I've been building Zaivy, a platform designed to help people figure out which business or side hustle fits their situation and what to do next. One of the biggest problems I ran into was that recommendations could sound personalized without actually explaining much. Someone might receive five opportunities with high fit percentages, but that doesn't necessarily mean they understand why those opportunities were recommended. So I've spent the past few weeks improving that. Zaivy can now collect activity-specific experience, compare it against reviewed opportunity requirements, and explain why someone's reported experience may be relevant to a particular opportunity. I've also worked on making the explanations more transparent about missing information and what the system can't confidently determine. The automated tests are passing, but I know that doesn't prove the recommendations are actually useful. That's what I want to figure out next. I'm preparing a small usability round with five people to answer three questions: Do people understand why an opportunity was recommended? Does the recommendation actually reflect their situation? Can they identify a realistic next step after using Zaivy? I'm also questioning whether displaying precise fit percentages is the right approach when the underlying model hasn't been validated against real-world outcomes. My question for other founders: When you're building a product that makes personalized recommendations, how do you determine whether users genuinely trust the reasoning instead of just trusting the numbers? Also, if anyone is interested in trying Zaivy and giving critical feedback, I'd appreciate it. I'm specifically looking for people who are unsure what kind of business or side hustle they want to pursue.

metadata.headline: I spent weeks improving my startup's recommendations. Now I need to find out if they're actually useful.

records.author_body: Hi IH, I'm Vadym and I'm building Upperdoc in public. The problem that got me started: small firms send a client a list of documents, half come back, and then someone spends the next two weeks writing polite follow-up emails. It's not hard work, it's just endless. So Upperdoc does one thing. You create a request with a checklist, send the client one branded link, and they upload straight from it. No account, no password. Reminders go out on their own at 3, 7 and 14 days until the checklist is complete, and a green/amber/red dashboard shows what's still missing per client. There's optional AI that checks uploads against what you asked for, but it only suggests. It never approves or rejects anything by itself. That felt important for people who are professionally responsible for the paperwork. It's early access: self-serve signup and a 14-day trial work, no paying customers yet. My question for accountants and bookkeepers here: how do you chase documents today? Email threads, a portal from your practice software, a spreadsheet? And what makes clients actually upload on time? https://upperdoc.io
